cards.back: One thing spoken of as another, with no comparing word. Effect: compresses an abstract idea into a felt image — name what the image adds that plain wording would not.
Comparison using 'like'/'as'. Effect: clarifies through the familiar; always ask what the compared-to thing imports (mood, judgement) beyond the likeness.
Human traits given to non-human things ('the wind gnawed'). Effect: dramatises the world's agency — often mirrors the speaker's state of mind.
A concrete object carrying a recurring abstract meaning beyond its literal role. Effect: binds theme to image; track whether the symbol changes at key moments.
A recurring image, phrase or idea across a work. Effect: threads the theme through the text; its final appearance often re-reads everything before it.

Theme = the work's central idea (stated as an argument, e.g. 'memory imprisons as much as it preserves'). Motif = the repeated device through which the theme surfaces. Never name a theme without the 'so what'.
Repeated initial consonants in nearby words. Effect: a sound pattern that slows, hammers or softens the line — interpret the sound, don't just spot it.
Repeated vowel sounds. Effect: open vowels carry (echo, distance); closed vowels thud. Tie the sound to tone.
Crowding of s/sh sounds. Effect: hiss, whisper, hush, or menace — frequent in descriptions of danger or intimacy.
A line running over into the next without pause. Effect: momentum, overflow, meaning arriving late — the pause withheld enacts the feeling.
A hard pause inside a line (often marked by punctuation). Effect: fracture, deliberation, a thought interrupting itself — ask what the break withholds or turns against.
Unrhymed iambic pentameter — the natural rhythm of English speech raised to pattern. Effect: dignity with flexibility; deviation from the metre is where meaning pools.
No fixed metre or rhyme; the line-break itself becomes the unit of emphasis. Effect: freedom is deliberate — analyse why the line breaks where it does.
Five iambic feet per line (da-DUM ×5) — the classic English metre. Effect: heartbeat regularity; spondees and trochaic inversions mark the moments of stress.
The turn in argument or feeling, classically at line 9 of a sonnet or before the final couplet. Effect: the poem's hinge — locating it precisely is a top-band P1 move.

14 lines: Petrarchan = octave (problem) + sestet (response), volta at line 9; Shakespearean = three quatrains + couplet, volta often at the couplet. Effect: an argument in miniature; the form enforces the turn.
One speaker addresses a silent listener; the speaker reveals more than they intend. Effect: dramatic irony built into the form — judgement is ours to make, not the poet's to state.
The speaker is a constructed voice, not the author. Effect: crediting the speaker (not 'the poet') is what earns analytic distance — and lets you notice when the voice is unreliable.
Word choice and its register (formal, colloquial, archaic, clinical). Effect: diction IS tone made visible — quote the exact word and its neighbours, never paraphrase.
The word's shadow-meaning beyond its dictionary sense ('slender' vs 'scrawny'). Effect: connotation choices are authorial fingerprints — name the exact overtone each candidate word carries.
Tone = the speaker's attitude toward the subject; mood = the atmosphere the reader feels. Effect: separate them cleanly — a bitter tone can build a wistful mood, and the gap is itself meaningful.
Sentence architecture: short sentences arrest; long cumulative sentences accumulate; inversion front-loads emphasis. Effect: rhythm of thought — quote the structure, not just the words.
Two contrasting elements placed side by side with no explicit link. Effect: the reader performs the comparison; the gap between the images is the argument.
Contrast set in balanced grammatical structure ('to err is human, to forgive divine'). Effect: opposition made formal — the balance implies judgement.
Contradictory terms fused ('deafening silence'). Effect: enacts paradox — a mind holding two truths at once; ask which truth wins.

Verbal: saying the opposite of what is meant. Situational: outcome contradicts expectation. Dramatic: audience knows what the character doesn't. Effect: distance between appearance and truth — the engine of satire and tragedy alike.
Early hint of what is to come. Effect: loads later scenes with meaning; on re-read the moment becomes a warning — cite both ends of the arc.
Opening inside the action, backstory supplied later. Effect: immediate stakes; the withheld beginning makes the reader assemble cause from effect.
A story inside a story (outer narrator, inner tale). Effect: controls distance and reliability — the frame's speaker mediates everything we trust.
A narrator whose account the reader learns to distrust (bias, naivety, self-interest). Effect: two stories at once — the one told and the one inferable; tracking the slips is the reading.
Narration mimicking the mind's unfiltered flow. Effect: immediacy of interior life; syntax loosens under feeling — analyse the breakdown as meaning.
Direct address to an absent person, thing or abstraction ('O Death…'). Effect: dramatises the speaker's solitude or intensity; the unreachable addressee defines the emotion.
Reference to another text, myth or event. Effect: imports the source's whole context into a phrase — misreading the source misreads the line.
Deliberate overstatement. Effect: emotional pressure or comedy; in satire, the excess measures the real fault it distorts.
Affirmation by negating the opposite ('no small feat'). Effect: cool understatement that trusts the reader — often irony in Sunday dress.
Substituting an associated term ('the crown' for the monarchy). Effect: compresses an institution into an emblem — the chosen emblem itself carries judgement.
Weather or nature mirroring human emotion ('angry skies'). Effect: externalises interior states — or, when clichéd, invites the writer's irony at the convention.

Soliloquy: alone, thoughts aloud to the audience. Monologue: long speech to other characters. Aside: brief remark to the audience, unheard by the stage. Effect: each sets a different contract about who knows what.
The purging of pity and fear a tragedy works toward. Effect: the ending's release is engineered by the whole arc — discuss the mechanism, not just the label.
The untying after the climax — consequences settle. Effect: reveals what the work has been arguing all along; compression or absence of denouement is itself a choice.

cards.front: The P1 move that earns marks
cards.back: Technique + quotation + effect-of-meaning, tied to the passage's argument. 'The poet uses enjambment' scores nothing; 'the run-over line enacts the mother's refusal to let the moment end' scores. Effect answers: why THIS device HERE?

Every paragraph: claim about the idea, evidence from work A, evidence from work B, and the comparison sentence that says what the difference PROVES. A difference without a consequence is a list, not an essay.
